name: 三点水 sāndiǎnshuǐ
explain: The squeezed form of 水 (shuǐ, water). Three short strokes on the left side. If you see it, the character is almost always about liquid, washing, rivers, or something that flows. One of the two or three most common radicals in all of Chinese.

name: 单人旁 dānrénpáng
explain: The side form of 人 (rén, person). Two strokes on the left. Points to a person, a job, a human quality, or something one person does to another. Extremely common because so much vocabulary is about people.

name: 口字旁 kǒuzìpáng
explain: A picture of an open mouth. Look for it in anything you say, eat, or hear. It is also used for many small grammar particles (吗 呢 吧 啊) because those are pure sounds you make with the mouth. Careful: a square shape is not always 口 — 囗 (wéi, enclosure) looks the same but wraps around the whole character.

name: 提手旁 tíshǒupáng
explain: The side form of 手 (shǒu, hand). If a character has this, you are physically doing something with your hands: pushing, pulling, carrying, hitting, holding, throwing. A very reliable radical — the guess "hand action" is right almost every time.

name: 言字旁 yánzìpáng
explain: The side form of 言 (yán, speech). Anything spoken, written, promised, discussed, or argued. If you meet an unknown character with 讠 on the left, you can safely guess it involves saying something.

name: 女字旁 nǚzìpáng
explain: A picture of a kneeling figure, the old form of "woman". Used for family words (mother, sister, aunt) and marriage words. Historical note: some characters with 女 carry old social attitudes that modern Chinese speakers do not share. Learn the shape, not the old judgement.

name: 草字头 cǎozìtóu
explain: Two small crosses sitting on top of the character. Always means a plant: a vegetable, a herb, a flower, a tree product. Medicine words also use it (药) because old medicine came from herbs.

name: 竖心旁 shùxīnpáng
explain: Two forms of the same radical. 忄 stands upright on the left; 心 sits flat at the bottom. Both mean the heart, and in Chinese the heart is where feelings AND thoughts live. So this radical covers emotion (happy, angry, afraid) and thinking (remember, forget, consider).

name: 走之旁 zǒuzhīpáng
explain: A long sweeping stroke that cradles the character from the left and underneath. Means movement along a road. Nearly every verb of going, coming, passing, returning, or arriving uses it.

name: 金字旁 jīnzìpáng
explain: The side form of 金 (jīn, gold/metal). Metals, coins, and anything made of metal — keys, needles, mirrors, machinery. Money words use it because old coins were metal.

name: 绞丝旁 jiǎosīpáng
explain: The side form of 糸 (mì, fine silk). Cloth and thread words, and also abstract words about tying, linking, continuing, and organizing — because a thread connects things. That is why 经 (pass through), continue 续, and 结 (tie) all use it.

name: 木字旁 mùzìpáng
explain: A picture of a tree with branches and roots. Trees, and anything made from wood: tables, chairs, bridges, boxes, buildings. Two trees 林 is a wood, three trees 森 is a forest.

name: 日字旁 rìzìpáng
explain: A picture of the sun with a dot in the middle. Because the sun measures the day, this radical covers both light words (bright, warm, sunny) and time words (morning, evening, season, era). A common beginner mistake is confusing 日 (sun) with 目 (mù, eye) — the eye is taller and has two lines inside.

name: 月字旁 yuèzìpáng
meaning: TWO meanings: moon/time, or body parts
explain: This one is a trap and worth knowing well. The shape 月 comes from two different old characters. Sometimes it really is 月 (yuè, moon) and means moon or month. But much more often it is a squashed 肉 (ròu, meat) and means a body part. That is why 脸 face, 胳膊 arm, 腿 leg, 肚 belly, 脑 brain all have it. Rule of thumb: if the character is a body part, the 月 is meat, not moon.

name: 心字底 xīnzìdǐ
explain: The full form of the heart radical, sitting flat under the character. Compare with 忄 which stands on the left. When the heart is at the bottom, the word is often a deeper or heavier feeling: 想 (miss, think of), 感 (feel), 愿 (be willing), 急 (anxious), 志 (will).

name: 宝盖头 bǎogàitóu
explain: A roof shape with a dot on top, covering the whole character. Means a building or being indoors. 家 is a roof over a pig (old sign of a household). 安 is a woman under a roof, meaning safe and peaceful.

name: 提土旁 títǔpáng
explain: A simple picture of a mound of earth. Ground, land, buildings made from earth, and place names. It also appears in words about increasing and piling up, since you build by adding earth.

name: 立刀旁 lìdāopáng
explain: The side form of 刀 (dāo, knife), standing on the RIGHT of the character — unusual, since most radicals sit on the left. Means cutting, splitting, or a sharp decision. 别 (separate), 刻 (carve), 到 (arrive, from cutting through) all use it.

name: 火字旁 huǒzìpáng
explain: Two forms. 火 on the left is a picture of flames. At the bottom it flattens into four dots 灬, which look like sparks. Both mean fire or heat. 热 (hot), 照 (shine), 烧 (burn), 灯 (lamp) all use it.

name: 贝字旁 bèizìpáng
explain: A picture of a cowrie shell. Before coins, shells were money in ancient China. So this radical marks anything about money, buying, selling, price, or worth. If you see 贝, think "this costs something".

name: 食字旁 shízìpáng
explain: The side form of 食 (shí, food). Every character with it is about eating or a kind of food: being full, being hungry, restaurants, dumplings, cakes, drinks.

name: 衣字旁 yīzìpáng
explain: The side form of 衣 (yī, clothing). Shirts, trousers, skirts, socks — anything you wear. Watch out: 礻 (shì, spirit/ritual) looks almost identical but has ONE dot instead of two. 衤 = clothes, 礻 = ceremony.

name: 示字旁 shìzìpáng
explain: The side form of 示 (shì, to show, altar). Means anything to do with spirits, ceremony, luck, or blessing. This is the one-dot twin of 衤 (clothing). 福 (blessing), 祝 (wish), 社 (community, from an altar) use it.

name: 病字旁 bìngzìpáng
explain: A shape like a person lying on a bed, wrapping the top-left of the character. Every character with it is about being sick or in pain: 病 (illness), 疼 (ache), 痛 (pain), 瘦 (thin from illness).

name: 目字旁 mùzìpáng
explain: A picture of an eye, turned upright. Seeing, watching, sleeping (eyes closed), and attention. Compare with 日 (sun): 目 is taller and has two lines inside, 日 is squarer with one.

name: 耳字旁 ěrzìpáng
explain: A picture of an ear. Hearing and listening words. 聪 (clever) uses it because sharp ears once meant a sharp mind. 聊 (to chat) and 职 (post, duty) also carry it.

name: 足字旁 zúzìpáng
explain: A picture of a leg and foot. Any movement done with the feet: running, jumping, kicking, following, roads travelled on foot. Related to but different from 辶, which is about the journey rather than the foot itself.

name: 车字旁 chēzìpáng
explain: A picture of a cart seen from above, with wheels and an axle. Vehicles and anything that rolls or turns. 转 (turn), 轻 (light, from an easy cart), 辆 (measure word for cars) all use it.

name: 门字框 ménzìkuàng
explain: A picture of a double door, forming a frame around the character. Doors, gates, and things that happen at a threshold: asking (问, a mouth at the door), being idle (闲), reading through (阅).

name: 页字旁 yèzìpáng
explain: Originally a picture of a head, which is why it appears in 头 (head), 颜 (face), 顾 (look after). The modern meaning "page" came much later. It sits on the RIGHT of the character.

name: 雨字头 yǔzìtóu
meaning: rain and weather from the sky
explain: A picture of rain falling from a cloud, four drops under a line. It sits on top and covers all weather that falls or forms in the sky: rain, snow, clouds, thunder, frost.

name: 广字旁 guǎngzìpáng
explain: A roof with one wall, like an open shed. Means a building you can walk into: shops, halls, courtyards, seats. 店 (shop), 座 (seat), 底 (bottom), 应 (should) use it.

name: 力字旁 lìzìpáng
explain: A picture of a bent arm showing muscle, or a plough. Means physical strength or effort. 努 (strive), 加 (add, from applying force), 助 (help), 动 (move) all use it.

name: 反犬旁 fǎnquǎnpáng
explain: The side form of 犬 (quǎn, dog). Used for most four-legged animals, not just dogs: 猫 cat, 猪 pig, 狮 lion, 猴 monkey. Also appears in 猜 (guess) and 独 (alone).

name: 鸟字旁 niǎozìpáng
explain: A picture of a bird with an eye, body, wing and feet. Used for kinds of birds: 鸡 chicken, 鸭 duck, 鹅 goose. Simple and reliable — if you see 鸟, it flies.

name: 鱼字旁 yúzìpáng
explain: A picture of a fish standing on its tail: head, body with scales, and fins. Used for fish and seafood. 鲜 (fresh) is fish 鱼 plus sheep 羊 — the two freshest foods in old China.

name: 马字旁 mǎzìpáng
explain: A picture of a horse with a mane and legs. Riding and horse words. It is also the most common SOUND clue in Chinese (妈 mā, 吗 ma, 骂 mà) — so when 马 is on the left it usually means horse, but on the right it usually means the sound "ma".

name: 禾木旁 hémùpáng
explain: A picture of a grain plant bending under the weight of its ear. Rice, wheat, harvests, and anything counted or measured out — since grain was how people once measured wealth. 和 (harmony), 科 (subject), 秋 (autumn, harvest time), 租 (rent) all use it.

name: 石字旁 shízìpáng
explain: A picture of a rock falling from a cliff. Stones, minerals, and hard things. Also used for things made of stone or clay, like 碗 (bowl). 确 (certain) and 研 (grind, research) use it too.

name: 竹字头 zhúzìtóu
meaning: bamboo, and things made from it
explain: Two small bamboo leaves sitting on top. Bamboo objects: chopsticks 筷, pens 笔, boxes 箱, flutes. Crucially, writing and counting words use it (笔, 算, 篇, 简) because ancient books were bamboo strips tied together.

name: 米字旁 mǐzìpáng
explain: A picture of rice grains scattered around a stalk. Rice and things made from ground grain: 糖 sugar, 粉 powder, 糕 cake. 料 (material) uses it because materials were measured by the grain.

name: 双人旁 shuāngrénpáng
meaning: walking, going along a road, conduct
explain: Despite the nickname "double person", this is not about people at all. It is half of 行 (xíng, road) and means walking along a path. It appears in 很 (very), 得 (get), 往 (toward), 律 (law, from a rule you walk by).

name: 耳刀旁 ěrdāopáng
explain: Another useful trap. The same shape means different things depending on which side it is on. On the LEFT it is 阜 (fù, mound) and means hills, walls, or steps: 阳 sun-facing slope, 院 courtyard, 陪 accompany. On the RIGHT it is 邑 (yì, city) and means a town or region: 都 city, 部 district, 邮 post.

name: 两点水 liǎngdiǎnshuǐ
explain: Two dots instead of the three dots of 氵. Two dots means frozen water — ice and cold. 冷 (cold), 冰 (ice), 凉 (cool), 冬 (winter) all use it. An easy pair to remember: three drops = liquid, two drops = ice.

name: 反文旁 fǎnwénpáng
explain: A hand holding a stick, sitting on the right. Means causing an action, often forcefully. 教 (teach, once by discipline), 放 (release), 收 (gather), 改 (change), 敢 (dare) all use it. Think of it as "making something happen".

name: 王字旁 wángzìpáng
explain: It looks like 王 (wáng, king) but on the left side of a character it is almost always 玉 (yù, jade) with its dot dropped. So it means jade and precious stones: 现 (appear, from polished jade), 班 (class, from splitting jade), 球 (ball), 玩 (play).

name: 穴宝盖 xuébǎogài
explain: A roof with two legs, like the mouth of a cave. Means a hole or hollow space. 空 (empty, sky), 穷 (poor, from a cramped cave), 窗 (window), 究 (investigate, from digging into a hole).
